method: The driver (elevated) created the test sublayer S2 and its provider with no filter, a Users-readable folder holding the probe and its arming proof (bound to the exe's own hash, 24 h), and a drop folder the account and the operator could write. The Lead Architect then launched the probe himself: condition F three-plus times as the account through Windows' secondary logon (a filtered token); condition E first through an elevation request made from inside the account's own console (route 1), then, in a second run the same morning, through a scheduled task he created in Task Scheduler running as the account whether logged on or not with highest privileges, the batch-logon right granted by hand in Local Security Policy (route 2, a batch logon that Windows does not split); condition S from his own non-elevated console; condition A from his elevated console. Each run read its own token (user SID, every group with attributes, integrity, elevation type, linked token, session), checked the stale SID resolves to no account, then made ONE FwpmFilterAdd0 (persistent block in S2 keyed to the stale SID, fixed key), a read-back, ONE FwpmFilterDeleteByKey0, a read-back, and wrote a record. -Collect validated every record (schema, hashes, condition, account, token state per condition, clock window) and -Finish removed everything by key and verified by direct reads and a netsh export. The account was created, enabled, removed from the group, deleted and its profile deleted, and the task and the right created and removed, by the Lead Architect in Windows' own tools; no script touched any account, task or right.

results.engine_access_list: read by netsh wfp show security type=engine at each -Prepare and -Finish, identical every time; the group's ACE (A;;0x307ff;;;NO) present as on 2026-10-13
results.reading: The group's effect on the engine is a property of the token, not of the account. Under an ordinary launch on this build the member's token carries the group marked deny-only, exactly like a filtered administrator token, and the engine refuses the add. Under a batch logon (a scheduled task running as the member) the token carries the group enabled and the engine accepts the add and the delete: the ACE applies to that token, as Microsoft documents for the engine's access list. The over-the-shoulder elevation prompt does not offer a non-administrator its own full token, so the route to the enabled token was a logon that is never split, created by hand. Not a finding; no disclosure routing.
